10500:
Steve wrote:
>>
Michael Di Salvo over at AtariAge contacted me about the possibility of a bank switched homebrew PCB for making larger Astrocade games.
>>

Thanks to Michael for asking about that... and thank you Steve for being interested enough to take a gander over here.

>>
I've read the discussions so far and taken a look at the Astrocade schematics and executive disassembly.
>>

Okay, maybe you took more than a "gander."  If you need help finding anything on BallyAlley.com, then please ask me.  If something that you need ISN'T on the website, then maybe I have it in my collection or any questions can be answered here.

>>
I haven't laid out a schematic yet, but I believe it should be possible make a PCB that has 32 4K banks and one fixed 4K bank, which would work similarly to 'mega-cart' bank switching on the Colecovision.
>>

I was thinking along the lines of 64K... but 128K is even better.  This has really got me excited!

>>
I haven't even written any software for the Astrocade, so I'll leave the question open to more experienced people, is 128K enough and is a 4K/4K system workable?
>>

a 4K/4K bankswitch method was s exactly what I was suggesting in a recent post.

Just a bit of trivia here.  Wasn't Atari 2600 Asteroids the first 8K ROM for the Atari VCS?  That used a 4K/4K scheme back in 1981.  So, the Bally would finally be catching up.  Well, sorta.  The Bally always had 8K available, but it never had a cartridge bankswitching method.

>>
Using smaller banks would require more parts.
>>

What would be the advantage of using smaller banks?

>>
I believe a 4K/4K system will fit completely in a GAL22V10
>>

I wasn't aware of what that part was until I looked it up.  If anyone is wondering, it's a type of Programmable Logic Device (PLD).  This would do the address decoding, right?

>>
and also accommodate inputs for a second PCB connection so the device can be flash programmed using a Maxflash USB programmer.
>>

So, this would be set-up like the Atari 8-bit flash carts rather than the Colecovision Flash cart?  The Atari Flash cart, as I've said before, is just wonderful.  It does require specially written software for Windows though.  Steve, you would have to write something like this for a Bally/Astrocade Flash cart, right?

>>
If the design only ended up requiring the parts I'm imagining here, a production run of quality assembled boards would probably be in the $12/ea range for a run of 250 pcs.
>>

So, that's $3,000.  As a community, we'll have to figure-out SOMETHING to do about that.  Any immediate ideas?

Would these PCBs be populated?

Also, as Michael Garber points out, there is a lack of available cart shells.  I have a friend (who I've mentioned before) who is a mechanical engineer.  I've spoken to him about this lack of cart shells problem.  He said that it wouldn't be difficult for him to make the molds that would match the shells we have.  The trouble here is money.  I guess this is expensive to do-- but I'm not sure AT ALL about the amount of money that we're talking about.  I'll ask him about it.

>>
I'd be happy to lay out a board and give it a try, but I don't actually have a working Astrocade. If someone has one to loan/sell and is willing to cover the costs of a set of prototype PCBs, I can probably have a set of prototypes ready people in the group to test within a month or two.
>>

I know that some collectors purchase more than one unit in case one fails, so someone on this discussion board must have a spare working unit available, right?  As for me, I DO have two units, but they both each have odd some odd idiosyncrasies that would make lending either of them out extremely difficult.

How much do you estimate it would cost for prototype PCBs?

It is great to hear from you, Steve!

Adam

Michael Garber wrote:
>>
This sounds wonderful.  Considering all future projects were assuming only 8k rom available, this would open up a ton! 128k is gigantic.
>>

I love the perspective that we have in classic gaming.  This is perhaps the only place in the work where "128K" would be considered "gigantic!"  And yet... I know EXACTLY what you mean, Michael!

10502:
Adam-

I know we have touched on this before and no, I never did reach out to him
(never had a reason to until now) but Mike White did have 700+ aftermarket cart
cases for sale that time on eBay.  Unless he threw them out (which I hope he
didn't) I would think at least getting 250 from him would be another piece of
this project taken care of. 


I still have his contact information but I was hoping maybe Ken Lill could reach
out to him and see if they are still available?  I had thought Mike's stockpile
was where the cases were coming from for the Crazy Climber release.  If we could
get them for a reasonable price say $1 a piece just for this special project we
could always option the rest at a negotiated price at a later date.


Also, I had asked this question before here but got no response so I'll ask it
again in case it was missed: does anybody know the history of the Bally thrid
party cart cases?  Who made them originally or where were they purchased from? 
Does the original mold used to make them still exist?  If anybody could even
help point us in the right direction that would help a great deal.


I might have a source for OEM cart shells but it would mean sacking existing
Bally games and having to remove the labels etc.  This is NOT my first choice
for lots of reasons least of which is they would not be cheap.  With 700+ shells
unaccounted for we need to exhaust that possibility first I think. 


Having someone who can make shells for us is great Adam, but from what I know
with systems like ColecoVision the mold alone is the major cost factor.


I have spare systems I would be more than willing to lend to Steve for testing
once we get everything else sorted out.  It might not be a pretty one, but it
will work, I'll make sure of it.  I would even be willing to cover the costs of
the prototype PCBs once we get there. 


As far as the approximate $3,000 we would need to the actual board production, I
have an idea for that also that perhaps we can discuss directly with a few
others that might want to get involved with raising this cost, when we get to
that point. 


-Michael

PS Thank you Steve for joining the group and thank you for taking a stab at this
project!

The other trouble with this is that the cartridge shells by Bally (but NOT the third-party shells) are made of a plastic that is brittle.  When removing the screws it is possible to strip the threads in the plastic.  The REAL trouble though is when re-inserting the screws into the cartridge.  Unless you turn the screws OUT before you start screwing the screw IN, you will get a stripped cartridge EVERY time.  Even following precautions it is possible to strip the screws.  This is just one of the reasons why it would be great to have new cart shells available.

10514:
>
> What would be the advantage of using smaller banks?

A larger contiguous code area, 6k/2k or 7k/1k instead of 4k/4k.

Almost certainly not worth the trouble/cost of an extra component unless there is a compelling reason for it.

> I wasn't aware of what that part was until I looked it up.  If anyone is wondering, it's a type of Programmable Logic Device (PLD).  This would do the address decoding, right?

Yes, for this design it would do everything, the hotspot decoding, bank latches and have a disable so the board could be programmed via a second edge connector using the Maxflash USB programmer.

> So, this would be set-up like the Atari 8-bit flash carts rather than the Colecovision Flash cart? 

Yes, I was thinking of a low cost board for mass production of new Bally Astrocade games, not a general purpose multi-cart type device.

A SD style multi-cart could be done, but it would probably make more sense to make one after a decent homebrew board was available to emulate, rather than before.

> The Atari Flash cart, as I've said before, is just wonderful.  It does require specially written software for Windows though.  Steve, you would have to write something like this for a Bally/Astrocade Flash cart, right?

If the board was made I would add an option to the existing Maxflash Studio software that could be used to program the Bally flash board.

It would not use the whole complicated multi-cart creation system thats present in the Maxflash Studio software for the 8-bit, it would just be a 'program board from rom image' option.

The reason I would integrate it into the Maxflash Studio software is that the program already contains all the code needed to interface with the Maxflash USB programmer.

> So, that's $3,000.  As a community, we'll have to figure-out SOMETHING to do about that.  Any immediate ideas?
>
> Would these PCBs be populated?

The $12/ea number is an educated guess as to the cost of complete, assembled PCBs with parts on them, delivered to us ready to use.

Parts, boards, stencil and assembly quote could only be finalized at the time of production.

> Also, as Michael Garber points out, there is a lack of available cart shells.  I have a friend (who I've mentioned before) who is a mechanical engineer.  I've spoken to him about this lack of cart shells problem.  He said that it wouldn't be difficult for him to make the molds that would match the shells we have.  The trouble here is money.  I guess this is expensive to do-- but I'm not sure AT ALL about the amount of money that we're talking about.  I'll ask him about it.

Injection molds are a whole new level of expensive.  I've designed and produced molds before for the Atari 8-bit and a few other side projects.

I would expect it to cost $300 or so to pay a CAD person experienced with injection molding to make 'ready for production' models of an existing case.  The actual mold costs, assuming its a straight pull two cavity mold might be in the $5000-$8000 range.

The actual mold cost can be highly variable and depends a lot on things like where its done, how much fine texture you need (photo etching vs bead blasting) and if you want actual possession of the mold afterward.

We would have to get to the stage of having actual CAD models to get hard quotes.  I can help with both of these things if you actually want to do it.

> I know that some collectors purchase more than one unit in case one fails, so someone on this discussion board must have a spare working unit available, right?  As for me, I DO have two units, but they both each have odd some odd idiosyncrasies that would make lending either of them out extremely difficult.
>
> How much do you estimate it would cost for prototype PCBs?

I would need a working unit to make timing measurements and a couple common games to make detailed PCB measurements to get started.

I think I could get 5 finish quality prototypes for about $160, which would include the flash and GAL parts cost.  I would have to hand assemble the prototypes.

After they were tested and working here and support was added to the Maxflash studio software to program them, they would need to be tested on as many volunteers Astrocade units as possible to make sure there were no compatibility problems.

The first step is basically to get a working console and a few common games that can be disassembled.

Steve

10530:
A trick that a lot pf programmers used to do to save space ib AstroBASIC
programs was to pre-load certain variables, They could do this because all
variables were saved during taping. as soon as you load this tape, print Y to
see where it is sending you. If it is zero or not one of the line numbers, then
the input byte is bad in line 34 and Y is not the variable intended here.

At quick glance, There are 2 ways to save 2 more precious bytes, AND a little
stack space. In line 32 there is:

32 .....;if G=Emul Fgosub R;return

33 return

if you change the gosub R;return   to goto R this will save stack space and 2
bytes. the return is in subroutine R.
If you were to just eliminate the ;return from 32, the return in line 33 would
do the same, regardless. this won't save the stack space, but it does save the 2
bytes.

Another space saver is here:

452 if L<4gosub L+1;if E>Fgosub P;goto V
455 if L=4gosub 6;if E>Fgosub P;goto V
460 goto 452

(47 bytes total)


452 If L<4gosub L+1;goto 456
455 gosub 6
456 if E>Fgosub P;goto V
460 goto 452

(40 bytes total)

Because L is limited to the range of 1 to 4 in lines 25 an 26, the if statement
is not needed in 455.
Both lines 452 and 455 have the same "if" statement so it only needs to be
defined once. By putting the goto 456 in place of that statement, you save 5
bytes in that line. You eliminate an if statement in line line 455 which saves
you 4 more bytes. however, by replacing the semicolon in line 455 with a line
number (456) you lose a byte and you also lose a byte for the carriage return at
the end of 456. total savings here, 7 bytes and the code is effectually the the
same.

To further save space, this is the least number iv bytes to use

452 gosub L+1+(L=4);if E<=Fgoto 452
455 gosub P;goto V

Now, try to figure out why this works and how many more bytes are saved.

I added 300-Baud conversion of "Memory Maze" by Steve Walters.  This program is now usable under AstroBASIC.  Quite a few changes had to be made in order to get this to work, they are noted below.  The biggest change is that the game runs quite a bit faster, which is fantastic because the maze generates in about half the time now.

These are the directions that appear on the screen when the game loads: "Study the maze until it disappears.  Move through the invisible maze.  Lose one point if you bump into the walls, and three points if you must peek at the maze."

"Memory Maze" can be downloaded here:

http://tinyurl.com/3h5ujp7

(or use the full URL:)

http://www.ballyalley.com/program_downloads/2000_baud_programs/misc/steve_walters/Memory%20Maze%20(1980)(Steve%20Walters).zip

This AstroBASIC game has been converted from the original Bally BASIC 300-Baud format to 2000-Baud.  It now loads in about twenty seconds rather than three and a half minutes.

Changes Made:
-------------

1)  This program was processed with Jay Fenton's "300 Baud to 2000 Baud Tape Conversion Program."  The program mistook "(C) 1980 S L Walters" to be line 1980.  That erroneous line was removed.

2) After the 300 baud BASIC program finishes loading, the "tape" continues to load four direct commands.  These had to be saved along with the 2000-baud version of the program.  The commands are:
     &(9)=168
     &(20)=129
     NT=0
     BC=133

3) NT=-1 was added to the beginning of line 100 in order to make the sound as intended.

4) The 300 baud "tape" ends with brief instructions that are comments.  Richard Degler took these instructions and made a title screen that now provides them.  The title screen was added to the program using Mike White's Blue Ram BASIC "Repacker" program.

5) AstroBASIC runs faster than Bally BASIC.  In this case the drawing of the maze has been given a speed boost.  The maze now draws about twice as fast.  This is a much-needed improvement because the maze is redrawn whenever the player "peeks" at it.  While it isn't unusual to see performance increases with AstroBASIC, this boost seems to work particularly well.

6) The program now autoruns when loaded with :INPUT.  This is because rather than saving the program with :PRINT, the program was saved with this direct command:
     PRINT ";RUN ";:PRINT %(16384),1887
This command is provided in Mike White's BASIC article "Tricks of the Trade, Tutorial #3"

Enjoy!

I added a court document from August 1980 called "Bally Manufacturing Corporation Vs. JS&A Group, Inc." to BallyAlley.com.  This document was discovered by Paul Thacker using Google Books.  I visited the local university law library this past January to dig it out, blow off the dust, and then scan it.  The document is seven pages long.  There is TONS of information in it, including:

1) One-third of all Bally Arcades sold by JS&A were defective and had to be returned.  We all knew that the number of consoles that overheated was high.  Now we have clear evidence (literally) of just how high the return rate was of the units.

2) Only 3,000 Bally Arcades were sold by JS&A.  The most accepted number of total Bally/Astrocade units sold is 300,000.  This means that only 1% of all Bally/Astrocade were sold through JS&A-- just a drop in the bucket!  These would most likely be the units with the red button and the earliest On-Board ROM.

3) Full explanation of the unusual story behind the "Bally for two-cents" ads that ran in the Wall Street Journal.

There is MUCH more included information.  I created a text summary of the document by excerpting part of the document.  This summary contains the information most likely to be of interest to Bally/Astrocade fans.  This is NOT to say that more information isn't available in the court document (for there certainly IS more information), but as a reader you will have to start digging through it and looking past the language of the courts, which, naturally, gets quite thick at times.

This is a list of software packages that have been received by BYTE Publications during the past month. "It is unclear from the snippet I can read whether or not this is simply identical to what we are defendant" should read "...identical to what we already have."  I must have had lawsuits on the brain.

In the Congressional record, JS&A frequently cites the Home Library Computer as one of their two biggest back order crises.  But they defend their handling of it, saying it was caused by the manufacturer, Bally, being unable to provide enough units.  JS&A claims that they went above and beyond the spirit of the rules in providing updates to customers and making it clear that people who had ordered it could cancel at any time.  JS&A did have a different interpretation of some of the regulations than what the FTC did.  There was a rule governing how long a mail-order company could wait to send out a product after accepting payment.  In the case of the Home Library Computer, JS&A accepted checks from some buyers, but held onto them rather than cashing them while they waited to get more units in stock.  JS&A believed that, because they had not cashed the checks, they had not yet accepted payment.  The FTC disagreed.

The site that has the Congressional record on-line is really nice.  You can do a full-text search, and switch between scanned images and OCR'd text.  It's actually an interesting read.  Joe Sugerman of JS&A seems like a colorful character.  He reacted to the FTC investigations by vigorously defending his company from what he essentially considered a witchhunt.  He ran print advertisements asking his customers to write to their Congressmen and to President Carter to defend the company.  He published a comic book, "The Monster That Eats Business," giving his take on the case.  It's copied in full on pages 371-418.  Supporters wrote summaries of the testimony, including the claim that Congressman Al Gore smeared Mr. Sugarman by suggesting that an article he wrote about "breaking the rules" referred to breaking legal rules, rather the conventional rules of marketing, as he clearly meant (page 648-649).

On page 427, JS&A explains their backorder problems, including the Bally system, and their interpretation of the mail-order regulations.

"The FTC considers a late shipment any check order over 30 days
old. Of the 21,000 orders shipped late, there were 8,000 orders
shipped over 60 days. That sounds terrible doesn't it, but look
at the facts.
The FTC rule states that you must ship a customer's order within
30 days or, if unable to, send that customer a letter offering a refund
which should also include a business reply envelope so a customer can
respond without any expense.
The second part of the rule states that if you don't hear from
the customer within 60 days, you automatically must issue a refund.
The rule only covered check orders unless you charged your
customer's credit card account and then the 30/60 rule took effect.
The rule was confusing to us because it really left credit card
customers unprotected. A mail order company does not have to notify
a credit card customer at all and can ship a product six months later
and not be violating the law. The rule did not make sense to us.
JS&A always notified all its customers of delays regardless of how
they paid and interpreted the start of the 30/60 rule to mean "making
use" of that customer's money by charging the credit card or depositing
the check.
The customers for the 8,000 orders over 60 days were all notified
of both the delay and the fact that we were holding their checks.
Incidentally, the orders were primarily for one product, a Bally
Corporation arcade game that used interchangeable cartridges. Although
8,000 orders seems like quite a bit, many of the customers ordered
several cartridges which were listed as separate orders, when in
reality the 8,000 orders were only, for a few thousand customers. We
even question the validity that 8,000 orders were late. A thorough
check of our records indicated errors on the FTC count and the FTC
won't tell us how they got their figures.
Deducting the 8,000 orders from the 21,000 alleged late shipments
leaves a total of 13,000 orders that were shipped over 30 days but less
than 60 days."

Home Computer From Bally
Byte, July 1979, Page 240
-------------------------

     The Bally Computer System contains the built-in "Bally Brain," a micro-processor that has a 12 K byte memory. Each optional Bally Videocade cassette adds up to 8 K additional bytes. Also built into the system are a five function, ten memory register calculator, 256 color display variations, stop-action pause control, and automatic shut-off. The unit is available in two player and four player models and has a 16,000 dot picture image. With three arcade games and a 24 key calculator built in, the two player model has a retail price of $299.95 and the four player model is $329.95. Both an optional Bally BASIC programming cassette and an audio cassette interface are priced at $49.95. For further information contact Bally Consumer Products Div, 10750 W Grand Av, Franklin Park IL 60131.

Ken Lill wrote:
>>
What people aren't getting here is if there is a cartridge made to go on the 50 pin connector, there won't need to be any bank switching at all!
>>

It isn't that people on the group don't get it-- it's that a cartridge would be a better solution for most people for several reasons:

1)  An upgrade device on the expansion port requires more knowledge of the Astrocade for the user.  For instance, most users will have to "break" open the expansion slot.

2) An expansion may not fit properly without some minor cutting-up of the area around the expansion port.

3) An expansion requires a hard-to-find, expensive and labor-intensive 50-pin connector.  A cartridge only requires the PCB itself.

>>
The only way you'll need bank switching is if you write code above FFFF.
>>

I agree with Ken that continuous memory is the way to go for programming, but for most USERS, it certainly is not the way to go.  A cartridge is MUCH more user friendly.

Even though this isn't a normally conceivable situation, a cartridge that has 128K of bankswitched memory could still use a memory expansion if it were available.  That would certainly be an esoteric game that used BOTH the memory expansion port for RAM AND the cartridge port for ROM.  Actually, this is so inconceivable that it is unrealistic except for a handful of users that have the Lil' White Ram.

 [...] With some of the games being advertised nationally as home computers, many people wonder just what differentiates the sophisticated game from the simple computer.  Two things - it is a computer if it has an input system for letters and numbers (e.g. a keyboard) and if it can be programmed by the user.  None of the 1977 games had these features, but several companies are now conspiring to screw up our distinction.  Microelectronic Systems Corporation is marketing a "video game" called INTERACT in 1978 that uses removable cartridges to store programs, and it has a numerical keyboard and joystick for input.  The company calls it a personal computer and plans to offer a program library that includes a variety of games as well as home and business applications in areas such as maintaining sales records, inventory control, income tax, and computer assisted tutoring.  The user does not have to learn BASIC but must take the programs as they are, without being able to modify them to suit individual needs.

INTERACT is a fourth generation game that is as much of a computer as it can be and still be a game.  It uses an 8080 chip and, at about $250, is a choice to consider if you want to be a consumer and have no interest in creating your own programs.  Two other systems which are similar to INTERACT are the Home Library Computer by Bally, an established manufacturer of slot and pinball machines, and the Apple II.  The Home Library Computer has a Z-80 microprocessor and provides the user with a wide variety of games and educational programs.  The thing even has sound built into the games.  When you shoot your opponent in a gunfight it plays taps.  Bally also promises a raft of peripherals in the future - items such as a standard typewriter keyboard, more memory, and a cassette tape system.  Its price is about $300 through JS&A National Sales Group, a well known mail order firm.

As it stands, the Home Library Computer is a promising video game.  The Apple II is just the opposite; it is a microcomputer which also has very good game capabilities.  Apple II has an excellent keyboard, comes with a powerful BASIC built in, and has the ability to read from and record onto cassette tapes.  That is the stuff computers are made of!  Apple II also comes with two paddles to make it easier to play games [...]

Bally/Astrocade related excerpt from Pages 59-60

Some video games are beginning to look more like computers as the technology advances, while some personal computers are also beginning to look more like video games.  The most glaring example of the merger of these two products is the Bally Professional Arcade, which claims to be a "video game/computer system" capable of "remembering more and doing more than any other system now available."

Actually, the Bally appears to have started out as a video game and gradually has become more like a computer with the introduction of optional programming capability.  However, its keyboard is a calculator style keyboard.  Entering alphabetic characters requires two strokes of the keys.  Perhaps, Bally will offer peripherals such as simple line printers and real keyboards and the game will become a real computer.  But at the time of this writing, I can't say this is certain.

Not all microprocessor games are video games, of course, and one of the more interesting of these is the Checker Challenger manufactured by Fidelity Electronics, which, like Bally, is headquartered in Chicago.  It is packaged in an attractive walnut case and has many interesting features including a "verification" key that displays the board position of each piece in case the pieces are knocked off the board or you get confused as to whether you've made a proper move.

I think that the slave is only needed for a non-RAM expanded Astrocade, and even then, only if you're using a menu for file searches.  So, ignore "slave" and "menu."  The version in the tutorial differs from the Arcadian version in the way that it handles file searches.  That doesn't matter though, as you're NEVER going to use that feature of the program (unless you possibly archive one of Mike's personal tapes).

Paul, since you have a RAM expansion, I would avoid the non-RAM expanded version all-together.  From reading the instructions, it seems that it works the same as the Blue Ram version ("Repacker").  If you've never used "Repack" before, then Mike's instructions probably seem a little vague.  while I've only used "Repacker," the directions seem to work about the same.  You should be able to follow my instructions and skip Mike's tutorials.  From my experience with "Repacker," reading the tutorials and the Arcadian, this is what it seems like you need to do:

1) I'm presuming (and HOPING) that you're saving and loading programs from your PC.  Before you begin, absolutely make certain that you have no trouble loading and saving AstroBASIC programs.  If you need to digitally archive a program in order to load it again, then you will HAVE to do that between steps that save, load and verify.

2) Have two "tapes" ready.  For this example, we'll fix Nuclear Math.  Have the WAV files of the old version of Nuclear Math (with the title screen) and the fixed version of Nuclear Math (without a title screen). 

3) Load and run "Repack."

4) When prompted "Awaiting Input of Text" then input your fixed version of Nuclear Math.

5) When prompted "Ready to load picture" then input the original version of Nuclear Math (with the title/load screen that you want to use/keep).

6) When prompted for File Search, choose NO.  This option is also included in "Repacker."  I've never used it.

7) Dump finished program to tape.

8) Play back finished program to verify.

9) If "Repack" works like "Repacker," then all of the above is a series of prompts.  Do what they tell you to do and you should be fine.

While I haven't used "Repack," my instructions are based on Mike's instruction in the Arcadian.  This is also EXACTLY the way that "Repacker" works.  This probably would have been a pain to do with tapes "back in the day" because of all the tape swapping, but it's quite easy to do using WAV files.  The only thing that may be a pain is that you have to remember to switch your cables back and forth during the saving and loading portions of the program.  I've forgotten to do this myself when using "Repacker" and it means that I have to do it again from the beginning.  If your Astrocade is setup, then you should be able to do all of this in about three to four minutes with these time estimates:

30 seconds to load "Repack"
30 seconds to load "Text" (Program)
30 seconds to load "Picture" (Title/Load Screen)
30 seconds to save newly interweaved program/screen to tape (the finished archive)
30 seconds to verify that the save went okay

The 8K version of "Repack" seems like it should be pretty-much like the version that I use with the Blue Ram.

Once you try this out, then anything that you're confused about should clear right up.  If you still have questions, before or after, you've tried "Repack," then just let me know.

Paul, let me know how it goes when you try this.  Also, Lance, you wanna give this a whirl and get back with me?

2) Have two "tapes" ready.  For this example, we'll fix Nuclear Math.  Have the WAV files of the old version of Nuclear Math (with the title screen) and the fixed version of Nuclear Math (without a title screen). 



3) Load and run "Repack."



4) When prompted "Awaiting Input of Text" then input your fixed version of Nuclear Math.



5) When prompted "Ready to load picture" then input the original version of Nuclear Math (with the title/load screen that you want to use/keep).



6) When prompted for File Search, choose NO.  This option is also included in "Repacker."  I've never used it.



7) Dump finished program to tape.



8) Play back finished program to verify.



9) If "Repack" works like "Repacker," then all of the above is a series of prompts.  Do what they tell you to do and you should be fine.



While I haven't used "Repack," my instructions are based on Mike's instruction in the Arcadian.  This is also EXACTLY the way that "Repacker" works.  This probably would have been a pain to do with tapes "back in the day" because of all the tape swapping, but it's quite easy to do using WAV files.  The only thing that may be a pain is that you have to remember to switch your cables back and forth during the saving and loading portions of the program.  I've forgotten to do this myself when using "Repacker" and it means that I have to do it again from the beginning.  If your Astrocade is setup, then you should be able to do all of this in about three to four minutes with these time estimates:



30 seconds to load "Repack"

30 seconds to load "Text" (Program)

30 seconds to load "Picture" (Title/Load Screen)

30 seconds to save newly interweaved program/screen to tape (the finished archive)

30 seconds to verify that the save went okay



The 8K version of "Repack" seems like it should be pretty-much like the version that I use with the Blue Ram.



Once you try this out, then anything that you're confused about should clear right up.  If you still have questions, before or after, you've tried "Repack," then just let me know.



Paul, let me know how it goes when you try this.  Also, Lance, you wanna give this a whirl and get back with me?

While adding RAM to the Bally/Astrocade is possible (and has been done by various upgrades over the years), the Astrocade can never have the graphics capability of the "arcade board."  The Astrocade comes hardwired with 4K of screen ROM, but it requires 16K of screen RAM to access hi-res mode.  That isn't to say that with lots of motherboard modification that the Astrocade can't be upgraded to hi-res mode-- it has been done at least twice before-- but it just isn't practical to do it.  With that said, here are complicated, quite-involved directions on how to upgrade the Astrocade to be capable of high-res mode:

http://www.ballyalley.com/documentation/hi-res_packages/hi-res_packages.html


Ken Lill actually has the hi-res upgraded Astrocade that John Perkins created in the early eighties.  Ken's unit requires a new power supply.  Once he has that, then he can dump the modified Astrocade ROM that was modified for hi-res mode.  Ken is the ONLY person that has a modified and I'd LOVE to see it dumped soon.

Here are pictures of Ken's hi-res Astrocade:

http://www.ballyalley.com/pics/hardware_pics/Hi-Res_Astrocade/Hi-Res_Astrocade.html


Rather than converting an Astrocade to hi-res, it would be better to buy an arcade board like the Seawolf II arcade game.  This is about as close as you can get to the Astrocade without having extras included in Wizard of Wor and Gorf.  Here are some pictures of the Seawolf II mainboard:

http://www.ballyalley.com/pics/hardware_pics/sea_wolf_II/sea_wolf_II.html


Michael also mentioned that he would like to see "game play [like the] arcade board."

With more ROM space, games could certainly be more involved and fun.  Compare the first games for the Bally/Astrocade to the latest releases.  Original 2K games like Amazing Maze/Tic-Tac-Toe, Dog Patch and Seawolf/Missile don't hold a candle to later 4K games like Galactic Invasion and Ms. Candyman.  The last batch of games for the Astrocade were 8K and included some of the best and most-loved games on the system.  These 8K games include Cosmic Raiders, Incredible Wizard, Muncher, Solar Conqueror, and Treasure Cove.  Mike's two recent homebrews, Crazy Climber and War, are pushing hard up against that 8K boundary.  The graphics of these 8K games are still low-resolution, but they each have more colors, better graphics and sound and a far greater depth of play.

Sure, a 128K bank-switched cart will allow for much greater depth of play.. but that's not all.  Imagine this... if you can...

More Graphics!
More Sound!
More Gameplay!

and...

More Fun!

That's what awaits you with this space-age, cutting edge, technology called bank-switching!

Bally.  You're Life Will Never Be The Same.

Bally "Home Library Computer" Advertisement

"Scientific American"

September, 1977, Pages 15-17



     Get Ready



     There are hundreds of new micro-electronic products about to enter the consumer market. Here is how readers of Scientific American can discover them.



     If you thought the pocket calculator started a revolution in 1971, just wait.

     In the next twelve months more micro-electronic products will be introduced to the consumer than in any other phase of the micro-electronic revolution.      This article, written for readers of this special issue on micro-electronics, will tell you how we select products at JS&A. It will give you tips on how you can evaluate a new product, and it will give you an insight into how you can keep abreast of all the new and important product developments.



An Industry Leader



     Our role in micro-electronic marketing is a matter of record. We introduced the first pocket calculator, literally creating a new industry. We were the first company to nationally introduce the LCD digital watch, and we are at the forefront of every major new product introduction, including a few you will see in this issue.

How We Select A Product

     1) Does the product use an integrated circuit? This has been the primary area in which we have concentrated.



     2) Is the product a major breakthrough or a new application of existing technology? (Both are acceptable criteria.)



     3) Is the manufacturer a solid, honest company providing honest value?



     4) Is the new technology in a product different enough to require the detail we supply in one of our advertisements? If it is not, then our pioneering efforts are not required and the product may not be that innovative.



     5) Does the product have advantages over the conventional version? Does it do its job more efficiently, faster and for less money? "Less money" is the most important key.



     6) Can the consumer figure out how to operate it without reading the instructions? If not, how badly is the consumer willing to read the instructions?



     7) Is the warranty and back-up service well thought out in advance?



     8) Is the product at least one year ahead of all other similar products currently on the market?



     9) Is the product a gimmick or an honest contribution of useful new technology?



     10) Can our company sell enough of the product to make a decent profit? If the product appeals to too narrow a population segment, then we cannot sell enough of a product to keep our margins low enough to provide good value.



Discover Our Products



     How do you find out about these products? Until now, to follow our company and its product introductions you had to be a reader of Scientific American or any of 50 national publications we advertise in or be one of our existing customers.

     In this issue of Scientific American are also a few of the products we are proud to introduce for the first time-- products that we feel represent the quality, value and the innovation associated with our company.

Teaching Device - Arcade Game - Musical Instrument - Home Computer



Home Library Computer



     The new Bally Library Computer provides more entertainment and services than man has ever dreamed possible from a single consumer product.



[Picture of Bally Home Library Computer]



     The handsome and highly styled Bally Library Computer is made of high impact clear plastic and imitation walnut with gold trim. It measures 5" x 11" x 15" and weighs five pounds.



     This is the story of an incredible product. So incredible that we know of no future consumer product that will have such a far-reaching technological impact on society.

     The Bally Library Computer is a small console unit that resembles a programmable TV game but whose computing capabilities resemble that of the IBM 5100 currently selling for $10,000. This calculating power and its present and future programs will provide more convenience and benefits than any other recent electronic product.



Electronic Printing Calculator



     Imagine the computer as a printing calculator with ten separate memories. You enter the data on the unit's keyboard, but instead of a paper tape, you use your TV screen to scroll out the answers similar to the credits on a movie screen. You can balance your check-book and then double check your calculations by scrolling back to your first entry. By comparison, an electronic calculator with ten memories alone would cost what this entire computer costs-- but there's much more.



A Challenging Teaching Tool



     Your child inserts a cartridge in the Bally console. Three random math table problems are then flashed on your TV screen. Depending on the speed and accuracy with which those problems are answered, the Bally automatically programs the computer with your child's math level. Problems in addition, subtraction, multiplication and division are then flashed on the screen for the next three minutes, and the computer continually adjusts to a level slightly better than the math level indicated by the previous three answers. The math tables, therefore, remain a challenge no matter how good your child becomes. Psychologists, who were consulted by Bally, helped design the cassette. They stated that the cassette should stimulate math learning and improve grades.

     On the same math cartridge is a two player game called Math Bingo. It adjusts to each player's ability so a parent can play against a child or two children can compete against each other at their own math levels-- both with an equal opportunity to win. You first answer a math table problem similar to the first exercise, and with a pistol-grip pointer you move a square on your TV screen to the correct answer position on your TV bingo card. The game involves both math skill and dexterity. Each game is totally different since the bingo cards have a million different possibilities. Scoring is constantly displayed, and a typical game lasts approximately three minutes. You can play as many consecutive games as you wish. However, to start the score over, you press the reset button.



Fun And Action Arcade Games



     Picture nine baseball players running out on your TV screen to the sounds of "Take Me Out to the Ball Game" as you step up to bat. That's the scene with Baseball, the arcade cartridge that plays two teams against each other with play so real that you hear all the music, sound effects and see all the action. There are double plays, walks and errors-- all part of nine innings of Baseball. On the same cartridge are several paddle ball games but with a new twist. Players can move the paddle, not only up or down like most TV games, but sideways and diagonally.

     Other popular arcade games include, Sea Wolf, Red Baron, Tank and dozens of games only previously available at arcades. These same games cost arcade owners up to two thousand dollars each.



[Picture of Bally Home Library Computer Circuit Board]

This package represents more computing power in the hands of the consumer than was thought possible this early in the history of micro electronics. More Value Per Feature

Excellent Business Tool



     With these expansion modules, business-men will be able to do all their bookkeeping functions, payroll, inventory control and billing. If you purchase your system from JS&A, you will be alerted to these new accessories by mail on a regular basis in advance of their availability and before any national announcement. You may then order the accessories directly.

     Each new cartridge or accessory will offer you a new way to use your system-- a way that would justify, by itself, the purchase of the entire system.



Not Just A TV Game



     Don't confuse the Bally Library Computer with the many inexpensive programmable TV games. The Bally computer is a powerful system using the Z80 microprocessor whose cost per byte (the measure of computer memory power) is even lower than a home computer. Yet it has 12,000 bytes of computer power in its most basic system and you are not just limited to' teaching, music, entertainment or business applications. The Bally computer can be programmed to do anything any mini-computer can do. A programmable TV game at any price is (and will always be) just a programmable TV game. It cannot be expanded. The Bally Library Computer is actually a computer with a variety of expansion capabilities.



A Computer In Every Home



     This is the first time a full-scale computer has been offered to the consumer. The home hobbyist with his home computer started the revolution a few years ago. With the specific programs, software and accessories available from Bally, the age of affordable consumer computer ownership is here now.



Internal Task Library



     The computer you buy now has within its 34 integrated circuits an internal library of over forty tasks that it performs. With such an extensive internal library, your computing power is already in the unit you buy. This also means that the Bally unit is a smart computer. (There are such things as dumb computers.) A smart computer can complete a function faster and more efficiently because it depends less on the data it gets and more on what it can already do.



Safe For Your TV



     The task library includes a built-in electronic timer which determines the end of a game or program by either score or elapsed time. It also times the arcade games and automatically turns off your unit and blanks out your screen if it is left on too long. Most TV set manufacturers have excluded sets that use TV games from warranty coverage be-cause of the possible lines that appear on the screen from sets left on too long with the same picture. This is impossible with the Bally. If you get a phone call in the middle of a game, you press the pause control which lets you freeze the action right in the middle of a play and blanks out the screen so you won't damage your picture tube.

     The library has sound effects so that each arcade game is complete-from the sound of a baseball bat to that of a torpedo hitting a submarine. It has a math program capable of turning your unit into a scientific, statistical or engineering calculator with the addition of the appropriate cartridge. The library contains the capability of creating patterns on your TV screen, playing music, and accepting type-writer entries. It even has an index that displays everything in your library.



[Picture of Bally Pistol-Grip Controller and Game Cartridge]

     The cassette cartridges add between eight to thirty-two thousand additional bytes of computer power to the basic 12,000 byte system. The pistol grip arcade accessory can be used to play all the arcade games.



The Major Breakthrough In Bally's Computer



     Its extensive internal library and the tremendous power in the computer are the big breakthroughs in the Bally unit. The internal computer has over 12,000 bytes with a minimum of 8,000 bytes in its cartridges. This puts more computer power in the hands of the consumer than six typical programmable TV games or an average hobbyist home computer. It has the computational capabilities of one $10,000 IBM 5100 computer, and each time you add a cassette cartridge you increase that capability.

By comparison, the best programmable TV game image is projected on a screen composed of 64 dots wide by 64 dots deep or 4,096 total dots. The Bally unit is 160 by 100 or 16,000 dots-- four times more-- so the Bally image is sharper and has finer detail, better resolution, smoother motion, and clearer letters for math or text applications.



Significant Expansion Modules

This ad was printed by JS&A, the only authorized dealer at the time, in "Scientific American" magazine in the September 1977 issue on pages 15-17.  Although the ad claims that the system would ship in four weeks, no customers are known to have received a Bally Arcade before January of 1978.



The pdf version of the document can be downloaded here:



http://tinyurl.com/3rm4cmw



(or use the full URL:)



http://www.ballyalley.com/ads_and_catalogs/jsa/Bally%20Home%20Library%20Computer%20Ad%20(Scientific%20American)/Bally%20Home%20Library%20Computer%20Ad%20(JS+A)(Scientific%20American)(Sept%201977).pdf



Since this is the first, quite lengthy, ad for the system, I went ahead and OCR'ed and proofread the document.  This ad is a very interesting read.  If you haven't read it before, then now is your opportunity-- as I'm including the full text from the ad here.



Enjoy!



(The full ad is below-- comments are welcome!)



Adam



Bally "Home Library Computer" Advertisement

"Scientific American"

September, 1977, Pages 15-17



     Get Ready



     There are hundreds of new micro-electronic products about to enter the consumer market. Here is how readers of Scientific American can discover them.



     If you thought the pocket calculator started a revolution in 1971, just wait.

     In the next twelve months more micro-electronic products will be introduced to the consumer than in any other phase of the micro-electronic revolution. Many of these products will 1) come from companies you've never heard of, 2) represent breakthroughs in micro-electronic technology, and 3) provide more conveniences and benefits than ever dreamed possible.

     JS&A has been the company most sought after to introduce these new products. Our national advertising campaigns and our system of selling directly to the consumer give high technology companies the opportunity to introduce new products to the market place in the most economical, quickest and most efficient manner.

     This article, written for readers of this special issue on micro-electronics, will tell you how we select products at JS&A. It will give you tips on how you can evaluate a new product, and it will give you an insight into how you can keep abreast of all the new and important product developments.



An Industry Leader



     Our role in micro-electronic marketing is a matter of record. We introduced the first pocket calculator, literally creating a new industry. We were the first company to nationally introduce the LCD digital watch, and we are at the forefront of every major new product introduction, including a few you will see in this issue.



     To achieve these results we have concentrated our efforts on doing only one thing and doing it well-- selling micro-electronic products directly to consumers through full-page advertisements in national magazines and newspapers.



How We Select A Product



     We have a comprehensive checklist that we go through for each product we select. The questions we ask ourselves include:



     1) Does the product use an integrated circuit? This has been the primary area in which we have concentrated.



     2) Is the product a major breakthrough or a new application of existing technology? (Both are acceptable criteria.)



     3) Is the manufacturer a solid, honest company providing honest value?



     4) Is the new technology in a product different enough to require the detail we supply in one of our advertisements? If it is not, then our pioneering efforts are not required and the product may not be that innovative.



     5) Does the product have advantages over the conventional version? Does it do its job more efficiently, faster and for less money? "Less money" is the most important key.



     6) Can the consumer figure out how to operate it without reading the instructions? If not, how badly is the consumer willing to read the instructions?



     7) Is the warranty and back-up service well thought out in advance?



     8) Is the product at least one year ahead of all other similar products currently on the market?



     9) Is the product a gimmick or an honest contribution of useful new technology?



     10) Can our company sell enough of the product to make a decent profit? If the product appeals to too narrow a population segment, then we cannot sell enough of a product to keep our margins low enough to provide good value.



Discover Our Products



     How do you find out about these products? Until now, to follow our company and its product introductions you had to be a reader of Scientific American or any of 50 national publications we advertise in or be one of our existing customers.

     JS&A will produce its first major catalog listing the newest consumer micro-electronic products that we feel represent the best contributions to micro-electronic technology.

     If you are a JS&A customer, you will automatically receive one. If you are not, we will be happy to send you our first issue. It is called "products that think"-- a collection of the most advanced micro-electronic consumer products.

     In this issue of Scientific American are also a few of the products we are proud to introduce for the first time-- products that we feel represent the quality, value and the innovation associated with our company.

     Finally, we owe a debt of gratitude to our customers and to micro-electronics-- the very science featured in this special issue. We are proud of our position in this field and we hope our contribution has helped both further this new technology and made possible the many conveniences now available to consumers.



Teaching Device - Arcade Game - Musical Instrument - Home Computer



Home Library Computer



     The new Bally Library Computer provides more entertainment and services than man has ever dreamed possible from a single consumer product.



[Picture of Bally Home Library Computer]



     The handsome and highly styled Bally Library Computer is made of high impact clear plastic and imitation walnut with gold trim. It measures 5" x 11" x 15" and weighs five pounds.



     This is the story of an incredible product. So incredible that we know of no future consumer product that will have such a far-reaching technological impact on society.

     The Bally Library Computer is a small console unit that resembles a programmable TV game but whose computing capabilities resemble that of the IBM 5100 currently selling for $10,000. This calculating power and its present and future programs will provide more convenience and benefits than any other recent electronic product.



Electronic Printing Calculator



     Imagine the computer as a printing calculator with ten separate memories. You enter the data on the unit's keyboard, but instead of a paper tape, you use your TV screen to scroll out the answers similar to the credits on a movie screen. You can balance your check-book and then double check your calculations by scrolling back to your first entry. By comparison, an electronic calculator with ten memories alone would cost what this entire computer costs-- but there's much more.



A Challenging Teaching Tool



     Your child inserts a cartridge in the Bally console. Three random math table problems are then flashed on your TV screen. Depending on the speed and accuracy with which those problems are answered, the Bally automatically programs the computer with your child's math level. Problems in addition, subtraction, multiplication and division are then flashed on the screen for the next three minutes, and the computer continually adjusts to a level slightly better than the math level indicated by the previous three answers. The math tables, therefore, remain a challenge no matter how good your child becomes. Psychologists, who were consulted by Bally, helped design the cassette. They stated that the cassette should stimulate math learning and improve grades.

     On the same math cartridge is a two player game called Math Bingo. It adjusts to each player's ability so a parent can play against a child or two children can compete against each other at their own math levels-- both with an equal opportunity to win. You first answer a math table problem similar to the first exercise, and with a pistol-grip pointer you move a square on your TV screen to the correct answer position on your TV bingo card. The game involves both math skill and dexterity. Each game is totally different since the bingo cards have a million different possibilities. Scoring is constantly displayed, and a typical game lasts approximately three minutes. You can play as many consecutive games as you wish. However, to start the score over, you press the reset button.



Fun And Action Arcade Games



     Picture nine baseball players running out on your TV screen to the sounds of "Take Me Out to the Ball Game" as you step up to bat. That's the scene with Baseball, the arcade cartridge that plays two teams against each other with play so real that you hear all the music, sound effects and see all the action. There are walks, balls, and such realism that the pitcher covers first base when a ball is hit to right field-- just like the real game. There are double plays, walks and errors-- all part of nine innings of Baseball. On the same cartridge are several paddle ball games but with a new twist. Players can move the paddle, not only up or down like most TV games, but sideways and diagonally.

     Other popular arcade games include, Sea Wolf, Red Baron, Tank and dozens of games only previously available at arcades. These same games cost arcade owners up to two thousand dollars each.



[Picture of Bally Home Library Computer Circuit Board]



     The Bally circuit board contains 34 integrated circuits including a Z80 microprocessor. This package represents more computing power in the hands of the consumer than was thought possible this early in the history of micro electronics. The mass production of these components and circuit board has made possible a quantum leap in lowering the cost of what normally would be a very expensive system.



More Value Per Feature



     Let's quickly review the features-- an electronic printing calculator with ten memories, a teaching machine that adjusts to your child's math level and an arcade center that replaces about $10,000 worth of electronic arcade games with just a few cartridges. Use any one of these features and you could justify buying this unit-- but there's plenty more.

     With all its sophistication, the Bally Library Computer was designed to keep current with advancing computer technology no matter how sophisticated the development. Bally has provisions in its present system for expansion modules. These devices will permit you to: 1) draw directly on your TV screen with an electronic wand in 32 different colors and eight shades of each color, 2) compose, record and playback music on an electronic synthesizer, 3) record your personal belongings and their value for security purposes and add or delete items while keeping the list intact, 4) record all your phone numbers and then use the system to dial those numbers on your telephone, 5) play chess on the phone with another player and be able to see all the moves on your TV screen.



Excellent Business Tool



     With these expansion modules, business-men will be able to do all their bookkeeping functions, payroll, inventory control and billing. There will be printers, telephone modems and a variety of peripheral computer equipment that will turn your Bally Library Computer into a significant business tool. And, when used in your business, your Bally unit is depreciable like all your other capital equipment. Even large corporations can use the Bally for specific applications to avoid tying up their larger computer systems.

     The Bally Library Computer will turn these incredible add-on features into reality in a planned program starting now. Each month, a new cartridge or accessory expanding the unit's capability will be announced. If you purchase your system from JS&A, you will be alerted to these new accessories by mail on a regular basis in advance of their availability and before any national announcement. You may then order the accessories directly.

     Each new cartridge or accessory will offer you a new way to use your system-- a way that would justify, by itself, the purchase of the entire system.



Not Just A TV Game



     Don't confuse the Bally Library Computer with the many inexpensive programmable TV games. The Bally computer is a powerful system using the Z80 microprocessor whose cost per byte (the measure of computer memory power) is even lower than a home computer. Yet it has 12,000 bytes of computer power in its most basic system and you are not just limited to' teaching, music, entertainment or business applications. The Bally computer can be programmed to do anything any mini-computer can do. A programmable TV game at any price is (and will always be) just a programmable TV game. It cannot be expanded. The Bally Library Computer is actually a computer with a variety of expansion capabilities.



A Computer In Every Home



     This is the first time a full-scale computer has been offered to the consumer. The home hobbyist with his home computer started the revolution a few years ago. With the specific programs, software and accessories available from Bally, the age of affordable consumer computer ownership is here now.



Internal Task Library



     The computer you buy now has within its 34 integrated circuits an internal library of over forty tasks that it performs. With such an extensive internal library, your computing power is already in the unit you buy. This also means that the Bally unit is a smart computer. (There are such things as dumb computers.) A smart computer can complete a function faster and more efficiently because it depends less on the data it gets and more on what it can already do.



Safe For Your TV



     The task library includes a built-in electronic timer which determines the end of a game or program by either score or elapsed time. It also times the arcade games and automatically turns off your unit and blanks out your screen if it is left on too long. Most TV set manufacturers have excluded sets that use TV games from warranty coverage be-cause of the possible lines that appear on the screen from sets left on too long with the same picture. This is impossible with the Bally. If you get a phone call in the middle of a game, you press the pause control which lets you freeze the action right in the middle of a play and blanks out the screen so you won't damage your picture tube.

     The library has sound effects so that each arcade game is complete-from the sound of a baseball bat to that of a torpedo hitting a submarine. It has a math program capable of turning your unit into a scientific, statistical or engineering calculator with the addition of the appropriate cartridge. The library contains the capability of creating patterns on your TV screen, playing music, and accepting type-writer entries. It even has an index that displays everything in your library.



[Picture of Bally Pistol-Grip Controller and Game Cartridge]

     The cassette cartridges add between eight to thirty-two thousand additional bytes of computer power to the basic 12,000 byte system. The pistol grip arcade accessory can be used to play all the arcade games.



The Major Breakthrough In Bally's Computer



     Its extensive internal library and the tremendous power in the computer are the big breakthroughs in the Bally unit. The internal computer has over 12,000 bytes with a minimum of 8,000 bytes in its cartridges. This puts more computer power in the hands of the consumer than six typical programmable TV games or an average hobbyist home computer. It has the computational capabilities of one $10,000 IBM 5100 computer, and each time you add a cassette cartridge you increase that capability.

     Good resolution on your TV screen is one of the end effects of so much computer power. By comparison, the best programmable TV game image is projected on a screen composed of 64 dots wide by 64 dots deep or 4,096 total dots. The Bally unit is 160 by 100 or 16,000 dots-- four times more-- so the Bally image is sharper and has finer detail, better resolution, smoother motion, and clearer letters for math or text applications.



Significant Expansion Modules



     The most significant expansion accessory will be the $300 dual magnetic tape decks with an alpha numeric (typewriter) keyboard. With this accessory package, which will be introduced by JS&A in approximately six months, you can record data and software programs and do everything you can do on any mainframe computer system within the data storage capacity of the Bally unit.

     The implications of this add-on module are mind-boggling. First, it adds an additional 16,000 bytes of memory to the powerful 12,000 already in the basic system. Secondly, it provides not only more power and features than are presently available in any home computer, but it contains peripherals that would normally cost thousands of dollars extra and are considered accessories on all other mini-computer systems. Thirdly, it uses the computer basic language which is easy to understand. And finally, each cassette tape in the system will contain an additional one quarter million bytes of storage capability. With the tape decks and keyboard, the consumer will now own the equivalent of an entire computer system complete with peripherals, storage and memory.



[Picture of Keypad]

     The Bally console keyboard is used to select specific programs from each cassette.



High Speed Printer



     A high-speed 2200 characters per second printer will also be available next year. This will give you written records from your storage tapes. Store your most frequently called phone numbers, your income tax figures, your savings account deposits, the value of your stocks and bonds or a net worth statement. Then, when you need the information, press a button for a printed record.



Dial-A-Bargain (R) Ordering System



     Our technicians have programmed JS&A's main computer so you can use the Bally to access our computer directly when Bally's dual tape decks become available. With a special module and cassette, you will be able to 1) call our computer on our toll-free number, 2) place an order, and 3) find out when it will be shipped. Since you communicate directly with our computer, your order is processed immediately and can be shipped within a few hours after receipt. To do this, JS&A engineers developed a $100 hardware ordering package that will be sent free to those customers who order the basic unit this year.



The Big Difference



     When you order the Bally computer today, you are making an investment in the future. The basic unit you receive, without a single accessory, will provide more benefits than any other product of its kind in history.

     When you buy an expensive product, you must be absolutely satisfied that you get the service and a solid company standing behind your purchase for many years to come. The Bally Library Computer is backed by a substantial company, Bally-- in business since 1931 and now the world's largest manufacturer of coin-operated amusement games. JS&A is America's largest single source of space-age consumer products and also a substantial company-- further assurance that your investment is well protected.



A Frank Discussion Of Service



     The Bally unit is a solid-state computer with its electronics condensed on 34 integrated circuits-- all hermetically sealed and all pre-tested for a lifetime of service. The Bally Computer is also self-diagnostic. We have developed a cartridge that lets the unit itself check every integrated circuit and every solid-state component and which displays any malfunction on your TV screen. Then all you do is send the circuit board or your entire unit to Bally's service-by-mail center for prompt replacement. The cartridge will be sent free-of-charge only to JS&A customers shortly after you receive your unit.

     Please don't think service requirements are common. They're not. But we wanted to assure you that service was such an important consideration in the Bally design that the unit practically repairs itself.



Complete As It Arrives



     Each unit comes complete with four pistol grips for use with the arcade and teaching games, an AC adapter (batteries are not required), three free arcade games, the calculator program, its internal library of tasks, complete easy-to-understand instructions and a one year parts and 90 day labor limited warranty-- all for only $299.95.

     The arcade games include 1) Gun Fight, in which two cowboys shoot at each other around cactus, covered wagons and other obstacles, 2) Checkmate, a one to four player game in which you build walls around your opponent to win and, 3) Scribble, a one to four player game that utilizes the pistol grip to doodle different designs on your TV screen (in color, if you own a color set).

     A keyboard lets you use your printing memory calculator and a special scroll button lets you scan your entries up or down to review or check your calculations. You may also order with your unit the Baseball and Paddle Games cartridge for $24.95 or the Math Table/Math Bingo cartridge for $19.95. A bulletin will accompany your unit listing all the other cartridges and accessories that are available or will be available in the near future. We feel so positive about this product that we will 1) not charge you anything for postage and handling and 2) give you a 30 day extended trial period to prove that the Bally is everything you expected after reading this article. When you receive your unit, reconcile your checkbook with the calculator, let your child practice with the math programs or have your entire family play the arcade games. After you have used the system under your own conditions and have personally experienced its fun and benefits, then
 decide if you want to keep it. If not, return it within our 30 day extended trial period for a prompt and courteous refund. You can't lose.

     Bally and JS&A have joined forces to mass market a product that will not only greatly influence the future of the computer industry, but will dramatically add consumer conveniences never before dreamed possible. Order your Bally Library Computer, at no obligation, today.

I don't think that anybody expected it to be a problem.  Later, a fake heatsink was added.  Bally attached the data chip directly to the metal shielding that was required for FCC approval.  It was this shielding that was causing the problem in the first place.  This "heatsink" never stayed put though.  On every single Astrocade that I've opened, the piece of metal that attaches the data chip to the shielding "heatsink" has become detached.  The metal is still attached to the datachip though, and this actually makes the heat problem even worse!  Luckily, at least on the Astrocade units I've opened, I've been able to remove the piece of metal from the datachip (it is simply held on with some sort of glue).

10654:
After talking to Adam, I was inspired to sort through some more of the documents in my collection. My initial thought was to just make a list of what I had. But after looking through it some more, I realized that it wasn't quite as overwhelming as I'd expected. Many documents were completely irrelevant, like a folder full of information on satellite TV. Others were quite uninteresting, like letters simply ordering a  cart or placing a subscription. Still others had already been scanned in some fashion, like the source code to programs that were printed in the Arcadian. So I ended up just scanning a number of papers and setting aside many others, and am now down to less than half a box unsorted. I think I'll just try to work through the rest as time allows.

I've uploaded a large number of scans to the FTP site. I won't discuss everything here, but a few items are worth mentioning. Perhaps the most interesting is a letter from the Bally Michigan Users Group which completely deconstructs a solicitation from the Cursor Group, all but calling it an outright scam. The Cursor letter says they don't have one dissatisfied subscriber, while the warning letter says they don't know of one that is satisfied. I had heard that the Cursor ended on bad terms, but I didn't expect something like this.

There is also additional information about Fawn Dungeon. Barry asks Bob for some information to help him out and talks a little about his plans for the game. There is also some preliminary code I'm not sure if this is different from the version we have dumped. Amusingly, Barry actually taped some cartridge parts to one of the pages to describe his modification of the cartridge hardware.

Bob wrote an essay for Kilobaud magazine called Arcade Resurrection. It describes how independent companies and programmers kept the system alive when there was a lack of first party support. Unfortunately, the magazine rejected the article as not of interest to a sufficient number of readers.

I scanned a small notebook from John Perkins describing his plans for the Blue RAM expansion.

There are several letters that Bob received. Probably the most interesting are some that were forwarded to him by Astrocade Incorporated. I guess they ended up getting a lot of game suggestions and etc. and would sometimes forward them to Bob to see if he could make use of them. One of them is actually addressed to Brett, and describes an idea for a Donkey Kong like game.

There are a few magazine articles that Bob copied or tore out. I enjoyed the one from Consumer Electronics Monthly. They interview Ray George, who describes his forecasts for his company's smashing success. Sales in 1982 are forecast to increase by 1000%, and to reach $1 billion by 1985. He says they have product scheduled all the way out to 1990. Of course we all know how this story ends.

Adam  do these look like the same sort of documents you have in your collection?

I also threw in a few Astrocade references gleaned from library databases (I'd already sent Adam a few more like this). There are a couple of good articles from the New York Times. It was good to see this system getting mainstream exposure like this. I also found a couple of bankruptcy documents, though I'm not sure if they add anything to what we already know. I was surprised to see one from 1987; I haven't really figured this one out. Were creditors still seeking payment at this late date, or is this somehow unrelated?

I think this should be enough documents for the moment. Probably my next upload will be more tape centric.

Paul

I've been lurking here a while but haven't said anything because I don't have an Astrocade yet.  I've been following this topic and thought I'd add my 2 cents.

A bank switched FLASH board wouldn't be difficult.
The circuit probably consists of just a memory device and a single GAL chip.  The logic programmed into the GAL would be some address decoding, a small amount of buss logic, and a latch (register) to hold the upper address lines to the FLASH chip.

To make address decoding easier, I'd stick with a fixed block of 4K and bankable block of 4K.  A single 8 bit register for the bank switching allows 256 different banks so you have 4K * 256 = 1024K maximum.  To make the circuit easier the first bank would be the same as the fixed 4K, so if the bank register is set to zero, the lower 4K is mirrored in the upper 4K.

Without looking at the schematics, 13 address lines must be present on the cartridge connector to address 8K of RAM/ROM/FLASH.
So A0-A11 go strait to the FLASH chip and A12 enables the latch output.  The latch output goes to A12-A19 on the FLASH chip and they would normally be set to a low value (not floating).

If Z80 IO ports can be placed in the cart then that might be the best approach.  So you have to decode enough of an address to get the I/O port in your GAL.  I/O ports don't require as much address decoding as writes.  Of coarse, if you use write, you have to decode enough for the address of a write.  I assume one of these is possible because of the BASIC cart with a cassette port.

However, if I/O or writes aren't available, reading from certain addresses in the fixed 4K bank will trigger the latch to input a new value.  It could get that value from the data or lower address lines.  I suggest the lower address lines since you could still put code it that page (256 bytes / pages of RAM like on the 6502).  That page of code couldn't use the upper memory bank since it would change during code execution but it's usable.
Either the first or last page of the fixed 4K would work best.  If you use the top page, A11 could trigger the latch input during a read when A12 is not active.  That makes a pretty simple circuit, actually easier than using I/O or write (if you fully decode an address for those).  Granted there might be some other buss signal required but like I said, I haven't looked at the schematic.  Programming the FLASH inside the game console would require more work and may require more power.

If you don't quite follow that last suggestion, the latch is loaded with the value of the lower 8 address lines when you access the page that triggers the latch load.  There are 256 addresses on a page and
the latch loads with a page number as follows:

setpage: ld a,SETPAGE+PAGENUMBER

Where SETPAGE is the base address of the page (memory area) where you set the page number and PAGENUMBER is 0-255 for the page you want to set.
The value returned in register a is whatever is actually in that memory but the latch is also set during the read from that address.
It's odd but it should work.  You could do the same decoding scheme with a write and it wouldn't confuse someone disassembling the code later.

Modern chips are pretty low power vs the 70s & 80s so the GAL + FLASH probably won't require a new power supply unless you want to program the FLASH inside the game console.



As for some of the system expansions mentioned in other threads...

For the video RAM expansion, if the chips were socketed that could be as easy as a plug in board with a single static RAM, a new EPROM, a GAL, and some jumper wires.  If you could remove the old RAM and ROM you'd need less power so no new power supply would be needed.

If you just want to tie more RAM to the CPU, that could be a small plug in board that goes in the Z80 socket and the Z80 goes in it... *if* the motherboard is socketed.  I doubt a new power supply would be needed and you wouldn't have to break out access to the connector on the back of the unit.


I'd have to look at pictures and schematics to say much more about any of this.

You're looking in the wrong place! Everyone else has pooh-poohed the idea of
using the 50 pin connector. You need to look at the cassette cartridge slot.
there are only 26 connections there.
A0-A12         13 pins
D0-D7             8 pins
+5V                 1 pin
Ground            3 pins

Chip Enable     1 pin

                       ---------
                        26 pins total

There is NO way to check for ports, no RD line, no WR line and no MREQ line
available at that connector, so those are out of the question.
Ken
