Ok, I've been doing research on the reset behavior and I haven't learned what I
want to know yet but I did come up with a couple things.

1. An I/O port is probably easiest to use.  No I/O ports above $1F (1FH) are
used by the built in hardware and all we have to test is the 6th address bit,
/IOREQ, and /RESET to latch the bank from the data buss.  It might not even 
require a GAL, two 74LS chips might work for a multi-cart depending on the
logic.

We also don't need to worry about what is on the data buss on reset in the
design, we just have to program the bank that is triggered on reset with the
startup bank contents.


2. Magic memory would normally preclude the use of RAM on a cart, but thanks to
undocumented Z80 behavior we might be able to get away with it.  It depends on
actual behavior of the Magic memory and the enable signal on the cart buss...
which I can't test.  Magic memory seems tied to /MREQ and /WR in low memory.
I/O commands use /IOREQ instead of /MREQ so I/O shouldn't trigger Magic memory.
And I/O actually puts the entire BC register on the address buss letting the Z80
put I/O anywhere in 64K.  I/O could be used to write to RAM or FLASH on a cart
if the cart enable is triggered by an I/O request to it's memory.  Just load B
with the MSB of the address and OUT(C),A to write anywhere in that 256 byte
block.  If that works, I'd use the high bit of the bank register to select
between FLASH and RAM banks, giving a max of 512K FLASH + 512K RAM.  That might
also gives you the ability to update the FLASH from code running on the cart
*IF* you use the right flash chip.  Add a special cable and you could download
data bit banger fashion through a joystick port to load the FLASH cart.  Then
you build a PC program to support it and could update the content at will.

I have my doubts that the cart enable works on anything but a read.

10673:
The circuit for the 4K + 4K banked cart should only require three 74LS chips and would be something like described below.  I make no promises since I haven't double checked it.  I just thought I'd pass it on before my attention span gives out.

74LS04, 74LS21, and 74LS373
inverters, AND gates, 8 bit latch.
The 74LS04 and 74LS21 could be combined into a single GAL.

74LS373 connections
Cart A0-A7 -> D0-D7
O0-O7 -> FLASH A12-FLASH A19

74LS21 pin 8 -> LE
tie CP high with a resistor.
/A13 -> /OE


74LS21
Cart A7  -> pin 1
Cart A8  -> pin 2
Cart A9  -> pin 4
Cart A10 -> pin 5
Cart A11 -> pin 12
/A12 -> pin 10
pin 6  -> pin 9
ENABLE -> pin 13
pin 8 -> 74LS373 LE

74LS04
Cart /ENABLE -> pin 1 --- pin 2 = ENABLE
Cart A12 -> pin 3 --- pin 4 = /A12

FLASH signals
Cart A0-A11 -> FLASH A0-A11
74LS373 O0-O7 -> FLASH A12-FLASH A19
Cart D0-D7 -> FLASH D0-D7
Cart /ENABLE -> FLASH /OE & /CE

10678:
Is the Astrocade's Z80 CPU socketed?  I already asked but nobody answered and I can't find a close enough photo to tell.

If it is, a 32K SRAM can be attached via a small plug in board.  Unplug the Z80, plug in the board and insert the Z80 into the socket on the board.

The board attaches the Z80 to all pins on the Astrocade socket but attaches the following pins to the SRAM (pin names on the RAM may vary)
Z80  ->  RAM
A0-A14 -> A0-A14
D0-D7 -> DQ0-DQ7  (data lines)
/RD -> /G  (output enable)
/WR -> /W  (write enable)

And you need this small circuit:
A15 -> inverter = /A15
/A15 OR /MREQ -> /E (chip enable)

And you can figure out power and ground.

When I spoke to Mike White at Ken's wedding, one thing he really emphasized is that we should be trying to find people who worked with the system to interview them and see if they have any archival materials while we still have the chance. I talked to Adam about this, and it was clear that our approach so far had been rather haphazard. In many cases, we found people simply because they've come to us. And even with people whose whereabouts we do know, we may not have any sort of formal interview. I decided that a first step was to identify who exactly was of interest, and list what if anything we knew about them.

I've now made the first version of this list. I've decided to take a rather expansive view of who is of interest. After all, we can decide later who exactly to prioritize, and I'd rather not go through everything a second time. I've included anyone I could identify who worked with the system for Bally, Dave Nutting Associates, or Astrocade. I've also included anyone who sold tape software,edited a newsletter, sold documentation, or worked on peripherals. There are a few miscellaneous inclusions, such as people involved in failed deals to buy the system. It ended up being 112 people in total. While I erred on the side of inclusion, I haven't included absolutely everyone. Merely having a program printed in the Arcadian was not sufficient, although I have included a few of the authors I found interesting for one reason or another.

The list has three parts  the name, the reason the person is interesting, and their present status. In many cases, the status is completely unknown. If we do know where the person is, I've noted whether or not they have an interview, and whether or not any materials have been archived. In a few cases, there has been past contact, but I'm not certain that we have up-to-date contact information. I've also noted when unfortunately the person is known to be deceased. There are also a few cases where I know of a person, but I'm not sure what their name is. For example, no one knows who wrote Dragons Castle. Also, we don't know who was behind companies like Cost Effective Computer Services and Winsor Computers.

10689:
I mentioned in the last message that I was getting improved results on a tape of programs by Richard Tietjens. Unfortunately, the results are still not perfect. In many cases, I believe the program is repairable. However, these programs are somewhat dependent upon the timing of the tape data, as instructions scroll by while the program loads. At present, there really isn't a complete solution to this problem. The Casio tools will filter a recording with the timing intact, and txt2prg allows editing of a program, but these can't really be combined together. It would probably be possible to hack something together by individually processing several segments of the recording and manually inserting silence, but this would be both imperfect and annoying to actually do.

I'm interested as to whether Ronaldo or anyone else has thoughts about this problem. The best solution I can come up with would be modifying the Casio tools to produce a new type of output file that included both the data and the exact time at which a byte occurred. Then we could modify this file with the correct bytes. A new program would then have to convert this into a wave file. It's certainly doable, but would take a good bit of work. Comments?

Paul
10690:
Personal opinion. The Bally system is very timing dependent. Inserting a pause
(silence) may tell the system to insert 0000 0000 there for the duration of the
silence AND when you come back to the data, if it is not timed right, you'll be
off from then on. Besides, how would you know if your break was at the exact
spot that a byte ended? That may insert a fault also.
Ken

The white chips were the early PROMS. The white area was ceramic material. The
later gray and black were made out of plastic. So, yes, the chips were common in
their day. The big problem was that you couldn't put a heat sink on them becaust
they had a brass square tha was elevated from the ceramic.
Ken

10713:
Hello, I'm Al Kossow, Software Curator at the Computer History Museum.

Jamie and I worked together at Apple in the 80's, and a few months ago I offered
to try to read the disks that she had in storage.

Over the Memorial Day weekend, I had a chance to get through about 2/3 of them.
The date range appears to be from 1979-1983. They begin with CP/M disks, which
were pretty easy to recover, but the bulk of the 'interesting' ones are stand-alone
TERSE disks, single sided single density 1K sector/ 4 sectors. I'm guessing they
contain the code for Wizard of Wor, Gorf, and Robbie Roto.

So the problem is how to analyze the TERSE disks. There is an early version under
CP/M, which might be a start. I guess a better knowledge of what exactly the hardware
was used in this time period that these were written on would be very helpful to get
a system simulation running for recovery.

The big unknown is what the 1983 hardware was, and why it seems to be writing a
non-standard sector format. The best I've been able to come up with so far is the
5" floppies seem to be 1K sector 2 sector disks, so I'm guessing it was also a
standalone TERSE environment.

So, any detailed information would be of help.

The good news is that so far I haven't had a problem reading the disks once I
was able to figure out what the sector format was.

So far, I haven't seen many disks with personal files on them. I am more concerned
about the later ones where I can't really tell what is there. One thing on them
is the sector data appears to be bit-inverted. There is text (ie. chunks of FORTH
looking code) once I do that.

10728:
The Terse disks are organized in 1K sectors. Files are not really a feature of Terse/Forth. They always used 1K blocks at the bottom level and access by 1K sector number. We built some file management on that.

JFenton, Lou Harp and I worked on BallyArcade ROM. Jeff McKenna came in as a consultant toward ship time to make Bingo Math cartridge. I feel like I may be forgetting someone. Rick Spees (sp?) worked with us but not sure if that was during the short Bally Arcade ROM build time.

Our original development system was a monster ModComp computer with tape drives. We have Mostek's Z80 assembler on it. It had no file locking so you had to call out MooseTech before starting a compile.

So we decided we needed a better development box. We made out own - Terry Coleman did a lot of the design on the Z80 probe along with Tony Miller. Jim "Gook" Hemmer (sp?) was master os schematics, layout and wire-wrap. Dave Nutting made the cabinets. They looked like baby coffins.

Dave Otto did some wire wrap, security, answering phones, baby-saf Jeff Fredricks (sp?) kids. Brett Bilbrey was much later in the game, about the time I left for Stern.

CP/M was in my sights all along because of my hobbyist activities on IMSAI 8080. I thought we could make a better cheaper simulator than the Tektronix box we had. We had a lot of contention to use it.

Timeline: Z80 assembler on big iron for ROM and some early game carts.
Tiny BASIC (originally by Dennis Allison for 8080, it was published in Dr Dobbs Journal in one of the early issues)
TERSE - based on forth but with faster inner loop due to removing a layer of indirection that Forth used.

The first TERSE dev systems used 8 inch disks.

A lot of TERSE disk sectors should be readable with "source" code in them. Once compiled to byte codes - no way - can tell them from data. The BIOS should be in the 1st blockd if it was bootable. I remember booting CP/M and then TERSE at one point along the way but I don't know if we moved more to CP/M later.

Best way to boot those disks would be Z80, 64K Ram, a serial port at 9600 baud.

As for bit inverted 5.25 inch disks - maybe they were from Apple drives? There were no 5.25 drives when I was working on it.

I still have an S100 system that works (or did last year) and an old H19 (heathkit) video teminal. I could go thru my collection and see if if I have any Forth/Terse related stuff. I kind of doubt it since I went on to writing compilers for my projects at Stern.

Let the questions begin! Maybe you'll jar loose some memories.
Alan McNeil (know as AL9000 back then hence a9k now).

10732:
> Who did the built-in games, or was it everyone working together? I'm a fan of
> Checkmate myself! There's quite a bit in the onboard ROM--4K for games and 4K
> for built-in routines, I believe. Did the inclusion of so many routines make
> programming cartridges easier, or was it mainly just needed to work with the
> custom data chips?

We thought of it more as 8K total and we had too much to squeeze in there all the time. I remember finding a tip from Bill Gates (and Paul Allen) in a SCCS (computer hobby) magazine that save a few bytes using LXI HL to "eat" MVI two byte instructions. I cooked up similar one using the 0xFD and 0xDD Z80 instruction to to skip loads. It saves a lot of bytes in "switch" statement kind of logic. My interest in peep hole optimization came from that time of byte crush.

The "OS" included a ton of helpful stuff. Events were handed off to the game via a table of procedure addresses. I designed it "object-oriented" where Game was a class. It was before object oriented was a buzz word. Objects on the screen were treated as instances of a class, usually with IX pointing at the instance data.

A lot of the inventiveness of our code was due to the severe memory constraints.

I don't remember all the games on the original arcade. I think I worked on GunFight if it was in there. Mainly because I'd just worked on GunFight II just before we started the arcade.

More later... I'm on a lunch break.
10733:
Yes, Gunfight is one of the built-in games.  It makes good use of the controller because you can turn the knob to aim the gun and push the joystick to move your character around.  The other built-in programs are Checkmate (a game where four players move ever-lengthening snakes around the screen trying to trap the others while avoiding running into anything), Scribbling (a drawing game), and Calculator.

Paul

10748:
OK, here's the scoop on those white chips. Back in the 6o's (I know that most of
you weren't even alive then!) They made most LSI chips that way. The gray areas
on the chip were actually the conductors that were deposited on the the white
ceramic substrate. The gray color comes from the silver used as a conductor. The
pins were actually gold covered. The black square in the middle is the circuitry
covered with a non-conductive epoxy. It was made black so that most lighting
wouldn't effect it. If you take an EPROM that doesn't have it's window covered
and leave it under any fluorescent light, it will erase it completely.
If the silver conductor managed to get a scratch all the way across it, you
through it away. There wasn't ant easy way to repair them. Now the silver
conductors are replaced bu a very thin copper conductor. (Like in the Z80).
The white PROM chip was made in the same fashion, except the conductors are
hidden, and the top piece is actually gold coated to make it 'rad-hard".
(radiation blocked).
Ken
